correspondence.component_scope: Northeastern opening and short head arm
correspondence.finding: The selected opening is in the southeastern head-arm cluster of the drainage labeled Agua de la Piedra, south of the distinct Incaguasi network. The original detailed map shows the initial northward elbow and its connection into the westward channel. The model’s short outer tip extends beyond the mapped arm tip, so only generalized head-corridor correspondence is asserted; the head-arm name remains unknown.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete at generalized head/component scale, without exact endpoint equivalence.

correspondence.component_scope: Agua de la Piedra upper corridor
correspondence.finding: Repeated labels occur on the westward selected drainage. Original map geometry shows the full upper corridor and the joining setting of the northern Nacimiento/Oreganito drainage and southern Bolsón drainage, followed by labels for Juncal.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete upper corridor and principal junction setting.

correspondence.component_scope: Juncal middle corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected route continues west-southwest along the map’s Juncal line, with the Ciclón and other eastern/southern branches kept distinct. The source maps its full southwestward bend toward the Carrizo convergence; the catalogue separately identifies Juncal upstream of the Carrizo junction.

correspondence.component_scope: Carrizo junction and Carrizalillo continuation
correspondence.finding: The original overview shows the eastern Carrizo branch joining the selected Juncal route, after which the westward corridor carries Carrizalillo labels. The branch joining and full western continuation are seen in the original maps, rather than inferred only from catchment membership.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete material junction and westward corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Carrizalillo and Doña Inés Chica joining setting
correspondence.finding: The lower detailed original map covers the westward Carrizalillo valley, the southeastern Doña Inés Chica connection and additional northern branching. The modeled line is locally offset toward northern side channels within this connected mapped drainage setting. The catalogue distinguishes Carrizalillo above Doña Inés Chica from Pan de Azúcar below it; no exact uniform-name boundary is assigned to model vertices.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete generalized lower valley/junction setting; no exact branch-alignment claim.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Pan de Azúcar quebrada
correspondence.finding: Repeated Pan de Azúcar labels follow the selected southwestward lower corridor. The maps distinguish joining Grande, Salitrosa and Agua Salada drainages from the selected trunk. CONAF’s original legend explicitly distinguishes quebradas from rivers, and its prose describes occasional watercourses in the park.
correspondence.correspondence: Complete lower dry-drainage corridor and material side-channel settings.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual Pacific terminal setting
correspondence.finding: The selected terminal follows the lower mapped trunk to the coast. CONAF’s original park map depicts the named quebrada meeting the Pacific beside Caleta Pan de Azúcar, near Playa Los Piqueros and north of the separate Coquimbo/Castillo systems. It supplies the sea/coast context absent from the hydrography-only white-background service; exact present mouth position is not claimed.

correspondence.component_scope: Headward seasonal channel west of the PE-3N corridor north of El Empalme, entering Río Llantén
correspondence.finding: The San Miguel original depicts a short dashed headwater channel west of the road in the Coimolache–El Empalme setting, joining the solid channel labelled Río Llanten. The selected southward opening and westward turn correspond to this feeder-to-river setting. The separate eastern arm of the labelled river is not the selected opening. The unnamed dashed feeder is not assigned the Llantén name simply because it feeds that river.

correspondence.component_scope: Río Llantén west through Quilcate and north through Catilluc, Challagón and Tongod
correspondence.finding: The original San Miguel sheet traces the westward river below Quilcate and Shilshil, then the northward bend below Catilluc and the successive Tongod–Callarco–La Lucuma reaches. The overlapping Santa Cruz sheet exposes the same river independently of the heavier CA-102 road symbols. The selected branch uses this river corridor; adjacent roads and parallel tributaries were not substituted for it.

correspondence.component_scope: Tongod and Yauyucan/San Pablo corridor to the Río San Juan junction near Ninabamba and Uticyacu
correspondence.finding: Santa Cruz maps the north-running channel from the Tongod/Chilal corridor past San Pablo, Yauyucan and Ninabamba, then the material junction with Río San Juan arriving from the east. The map prints Río Chancay on the selected north-south channel and on the receiving northwestern continuation. This supports continuity and that map's local naming, without establishing an exact legally defined Llantén/Chancay transition. The selected route does not turn east onto San Juan or Tacamache.

correspondence.component_scope: Río Chancay west past Uticyacu, San Lorenzo and Chancaybaños, then southwest along the Santa Cruz valley to Río Cañad
correspondence.finding: The Santa Cruz original traces the selected broad northwestern bend from the San Juan junction, west through the San Lorenzo/Chancaybaños reach and then southwest along the western side of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba. Its southern bend receives the mapped Río Cañad from the southeast near the road crossing north of Catache. Both junction geometry and downstream continuation are readable at corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Chancay through Catache and the Cirato and Cumbil/Maichil junction settings to Chongoyape
correspondence.finding: Santa Cruz and Chiclayo overlap on the westward Chancay valley through Catache, the tributary labelled Río Cirato, the Cumbil bridge/Maichil tributary setting and the continuation to Raca Rumi–Chongoyape. The selected river follows the mapped receiving trunk below these material tributary junctions. PEOT RG-01 independently places Chancay in this same corridor and distinguishes its southern Chilal tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: Chancay southwest through Huaca Blanca, Tablazos and Wadington to La Puntilla; Tinajones reservoir relationship
correspondence.finding: MTC Chiclayo traces the main river southwest to La Puntilla. PEOT's original RG-01 map distinctly outlines Reservorio Tinajones northwest of the selected river, while the selected channel passes southeast of the reservoir through the Huaca Blanca–Tablazos–Wadington corridor to Desaguadero/La Puntilla. Thus the selected line is not interpreted as a passage through Tinajones. The reservoir label in the generalized MTC map is not used to move the selected line into a lake.

correspondence.component_scope: La Puntilla southern branch into Río Reque, past La Vega, Pucalá and the Tumán/Chiclayo plain
correspondence.finding: MTC explicitly labels separate Río Taymi, Río Lambayeque and Río Reque courses at and west of La Puntilla. The selected southwestern branch is the Reque course, passing La Vega/Huaca de Piedra and then continuing through the Pucalá–Tumán plain toward Reque. PEOT RG-01 shows the same southern branch, distinct from the northern Lambayeque course and from the Boró and Collique reservoirs. The 2021 PEOT prose independently states that La Puntilla distributes water to Taymi, Lambayeque and Río Reque. Neither the northern branches nor those reservoirs are part of this selected mainstem.

correspondence.component_scope: Río Reque past the Reque bridge and Monsefú/Eten plain to the Pacific coast
correspondence.finding: MTC Chiclayo depicts the selected river through the Reque bridge/Larán setting and southwest across the Monsefú–Eten plain, with the Río Reque label at the coastal reach beside Eten. PEOT RG-01 also traces the same river past Monsefú and Eten to the Pacific, separately from Puerto Eten to the south. This establishes the actual terminal setting at ordinary generalized mouth/corridor scale; no exact present-day bank, estuary outline or surveyed mouth-point claim is made.

correspondence.component_scope: western selected opening
correspondence.finding: A blue feeder rises southwest of El Consejo in the Las Guacamayas area, runs north toward La Mora, then east into the named Tuy corridor near El Consejo. This is the selected opening; the separately mapped northern Tuy branch descends through the Santa Rita area.
correspondence.name_scope: The initial southwestern feeder is unnamed on this map. Do not extend Río Tuy upstream over it or identify the selected start with the northern Tuy source near Colonia Tovar.
correspondence.source_locator: Upper-central Aragua map, Las Guacamayas–La Mora–El Consejo area, with the 67°15′W and 10°15′N graticule for ordinary orientation.

correspondence.component_scope: El Consejo–Las Tejerías/Guayas–Boca de Cagua–Tácata corridor
correspondence.finding: The connected channel continues east by El Consejo and below Las Tejerías/Guayas, then bends southeast toward Tácata. The map directly labels the downstream channel Río Tuy. The field study distinguishes Quebrada Guayas and Río Guare from main-channel stations.
correspondence.name_scope: Río Tuy is supported for the receiving main-river corridor; tributary names retain their separate scope.
correspondence.source_locator: Aragua map upper-central/eastern portion; UPSE Figure1 and Table1 stations5–11.

correspondence.component_scope: Tácata–Cúa–Ocumare–San Francisco de Yare–Santa Teresa
correspondence.finding: The river swings southeast through the Cúa/Ocumare valley and turns north toward Yare and Santa Teresa. Mapped Ocumarito, Lagartijo and Quebrada Seca reservoirs occupy side waters rather than a required through-reservoir passage of the selected river. The primary field map and station table separate Ocumarito, Charallave, Marare, Súcuta and Guaire tributary observations.
correspondence.name_scope: No reservoir or side-branch reach inherits the representative Tuy name. Main-channel station Lagartijo is not equated with traversal of Embalse Lagartijo.
correspondence.source_locator: Aragua map eastern corridor and reservoir context; UPSE Figure1 and Table1 stations11–22.

correspondence.component_scope: Santa Teresa–Aragüita–Caucagua/Cuira junction region–Panaquire
correspondence.finding: The mapped main corridor continues east from the Santa Teresa/Guaire junction area, receives separately mapped Taguacita, Taguaza, Caucagua and Cuira branches, and continues by Panaquire. The field map supplies connected linework, not merely a Tuy basin outline.
correspondence.name_scope: The downstream representative river does not rename these tributaries. Embalse Taguaza is mapped on side drainage, not on the selected main path.
correspondence.source_locator: UPSE Figure1 and Table1 stations21–30; Aragua map eastern edge supplies overlap through Aragüita and side-water Taguaza context.

correspondence.component_scope: lower Barlovento plain and terminal
correspondence.finding: The eastern main river winds across the lower plain, turns northward and then northeast to the Caribbean coastline. The field campaign terminates at Boca de Paparo, which the study identifies as the river mouth. The selected terminal corresponds to that direct coastal setting.
correspondence.name_scope: The terminal finding is Caribbean discharge at Boca de Paparo at ordinary coastal-corridor scale; no exact mouth-point or modern shoreline agreement is asserted.
correspondence.source_locator: UPSE Figure1 lower-right corridor to station36; Table1 stations29–36 and study-area/methods prose on printed page49.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwestern opening below the Cerro Pintado sector and upper connector
correspondence.finding: The acquired regional overview places the headward Guasare valley in the Perijá mountain belt, and Figure8 locates the Cerro Pintado cave/karst setting. Neither Figure8 nor the relief-heavy Figure1 provides a sufficiently clear route from the selected southwestern start into the detailed middle-valley map. Prose naming Cerro Pintado does not close this material gap.
correspondence.correspondence: Regional headward setting only; actual entire selected opening and its connector pending.

correspondence.component_scope: Guasare middle valley northeastward beside the separate Socuy valley
correspondence.finding: Rodríguez and Galán Figure3 maps the long northeast-running Guasare valley, western and eastern side drainage including Caño Grande/Pan Grande and smaller tributaries, and the separate parallel Socuy corridor to its southeast. The selection follows the Guasare valley through this setting rather than the Socuy branch. The article describes underground flow in a Guasare interval, without licensing precise subterranean-channel reconstruction.
correspondence.correspondence: Primary middle-valley map read, with overlapping regional context.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward foothill bend and eastward lowland Guasare approach
correspondence.finding: The mapped Guasare exits the northeast-trending mountain valley, turns north and then east along the northern edge of the foothills. The separate southeastern Socuy/Cachirí reservoir-drainage branch remains distinguishable; the selected route stays on the northern approach.
correspondence.correspondence: Regional original maps read at generalized corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Guasare–Socuy receiving junction and Limón wetland approach
correspondence.finding: The regional maps show the northern Guasare and southern Socuy approaches joining in the lowland before the receiving channel enters the coastal wetland/lagoon complex. Rincón explicitly applies Limón after Socuy joins Guasare. The selected eastward receiving route is consistent with this mapped continuation. No precise naming-boundary vertex is claimed.
correspondence.correspondence: Junction setting and onward lowland/lagoon corridor read in regional maps; naming transition supported by prose.

correspondence.component_scope: Sinamaica-associated lower channel and actual Urubá terminal
correspondence.finding: Barboza et al. Figure1, prepared by IVIC UniSIG, maps and labels the lower Río Limón emerging from the Sinamaica wetland setting into Bahía de Urubá, west/northwest of Isla de Toas. Urubá opens into Bahía El Tablazo and the wider Maracaibo system. This resolves the selected actual terminal setting as the Limón estuarine outlet, without equating the terminal to the open Gulf coast or renaming the lagoon/bay passage.
correspondence.correspondence: Original terminal map and overlapping regional context read.
